note: Append-only. Ids are permanent: a case that no longer applies gets `retired` with a reason and keeps its number. Coverage is a CLAIM; scripts/case-registry.ts turns it into evidence by executing it.

cases.title: Prototype pollution through a request-supplied key
cases.rationale: A value the caller controls is used directly as a computed key on a write. Setting `__proto__` re-parents the object, which is the whole of CWE-1321. This is the shortest form the bug takes in real code.
cases.code: function f(o, req) { o[req.query.p] = 1; }

cases.title: Prototype pollution through an unguarded merge helper
cases.rationale: `for (const k in src) dst[k] = src[k]` over a caller-supplied source is the shape behind the published prototype-pollution advisories in the deep-merge family. The key is never named in the source, so no allowlist can be read off the file.
cases.code: function merge(dst, src) { for (const k in src) { dst[k] = src[k]; } return dst; }

cases.title: A computed write onto `this` inside a class method
cases.rationale: Reads like noise and is not. Verified by execution: calling the method with `__proto__` re-parents the instance. Registered so the finding cannot be dismissed as an FP a second time.
cases.code: class Bag { set(k, v) { this[k] = v; } }

cases.title: Array append written as a self-indexed length
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. `arr.length` is a number, so the key cannot name a prototype slot. Written with `arr` as a PARAMETER on purpose: a locally-constructed array was already cleared by an older path, so `const arr = []` would pass whether or not the fix exists — a case that cannot fail is not evidence.
cases.code: function push(arr, x) { arr[arr.length] = x; }

cases.title: A key iterated from a const array of string literals
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. Every value the key can take is written out in the same file and none is a dangerous property, so the question is decidable rather than assumed. An author who lists `__proto__` themselves still gets the report.
cases.code: const KEYS = ["alpha", "beta"]; const o = {}; for (const k of KEYS) { o[k] = 1; }

cases.title: A copy loop over an object the module itself owns
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. Nothing an attacker supplies reaches the loop. eslint-plugin-security reports this twice, once per side of the assignment; the noise is by their design, not a disagreement about the facts.
cases.code: const cfg = { a: 1 }; const out = {}; for (const k in cfg) { out[k] = cfg[k]; }

cases.title: Prototype pollution through a merge helper whose hasOwn guard names the source
cases.rationale: Reclassified from decoy on 2026-09-15. It was registered as the documented remediation for ILB-0002, on the reasoning that Object.hasOwn is the sanctioned guard. That reasoning was never executed. The guard names src and the write lands on dst, so it proves nothing about the object being written: with src = JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {...}}'), __proto__ IS an own property, the guard passes, and dst[k] = src[k] reparents dst. In the recursive spelling it walks into Object.prototype and pollutes every object in the process. It is ILB-0002 with a guard that does not cover the write, not its fix.
cases.code: function merge(dst, src) { for (const k in src) { if (Object.hasOwn(src, k)) dst[k] = src[k]; } }

cases.title: A timing-unsafe comparison of a bearer token
cases.rationale: `===` on a secret short-circuits at the first differing byte, so response time leaks the shared prefix. Observed guarding five HTTP endpoints in a real deployment.
cases.code:
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
function check(req, secret) { if (req.headers.authorization === secret) { return true; } return false; }

cases.title: An AST discriminant compared with ===
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. `node.kind === SyntaxKind.X` is a tag comparison, not a secret. Eleven findings in the wild came from this one shape before it was sealed.
cases.code:
import ts from 'typescript';
function f(node) { return node.kind === ts.SyntaxKind.ClassDeclaration; }

cases.title: Prototype pollution through a key reached by a call
cases.rationale: The key is computed at runtime by a function this file cannot summarise. Registered as an OPEN question rather than a claim: whether an unresolvable key should report is the same judgement as FP-010, and no rule currently answers it deliberately.
cases.code: function f(o) { o[getKey()] = 1; }

import cp from 'node:child_process';
function f(req) { cp.exec('ls ' + req.body.dir); }

cases.title: destructured exec
cases.rationale: Destructuring hides the receiver, not the sink.
cases.code:
const { exec } = require('child_process');
function f(req) { exec('ls ' + req.query.dir); }

cases.title: a fully literal command
cases.rationale: The command is written in the file.
cases.code:
const cp = require('child_process');
cp.exec('ls -la');

cases.title: execFile with a caller-chosen argument
cases.rationale: Written as a decoy on the assumption that no shell means no defect. Executed: `execFileSync('echo', ['safe; echo PWNED'])` yields the literal string, so command injection is indeed impossible — but the caller still chooses an ARGUMENT, and a leading `-` is a flag. The rule reports CWE-88 argument injection here, not CWE-78, and goes silent once `--` terminates option parsing. The rule was right and the case was wrong.
cases.code:
const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.execFile('ls', [req.query.dir]); }

cases.title: spawn with a caller-chosen argument
cases.rationale: Written as a decoy on the assumption that no shell means no defect. Executed: `execFileSync('echo', ['safe; echo PWNED'])` yields the literal string, so command injection is indeed impossible — but the caller still chooses an ARGUMENT, and a leading `-` is a flag. The rule reports CWE-88 argument injection here, not CWE-78, and goes silent once `--` terminates option parsing. The rule was right and the case was wrong.
cases.code:
const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.spawn('ls', [req.query.dir]); }

cases.title: a call to something else named exec
cases.rationale: RegExp.prototype.exec is not a shell.
cases.code: function f(re, s) { return re.exec(s); }

cases.title: the documented fix
cases.rationale: Reporting the fix leaves the user nothing to do.
cases.code:
const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.execFile('ls', ['--', req.query.dir]); }

cases.title: Cross-document message broadcast to any origin
cases.rationale: `'*'` tells the browser to deliver the message to whatever document currently occupies the frame. If the frame has navigated, or was navigated by an attacker, the payload lands in their document. MDN names this the primary security concern of the API.
cases.code: window.parent.postMessage({ token: t }, '*');

cases.title: A concrete target origin
cases.rationale: The same call with an origin the browser must match before delivering. Looks identical in shape to the defect and must stay quiet — this is the form the fix takes.
cases.code: window.parent.postMessage({ token: t }, 'https://app.example.com');

cases.title: A wildcard string that is not a target origin
cases.rationale: `'*'` appearing as the message BODY rather than the origin argument. A rule matching the literal without regard to argument position reports this.
cases.code: window.parent.postMessage('*', 'https://app.example.com');

cases.title: Request object spread straight into a Mongo filter
cases.rationale: A caller-controlled object becomes the query document. `{"$ne": null}` as a password turns the lookup into 'any user', which is the canonical NoSQL authentication bypass. Missed until 2026-08-30: the rule early-returned on any first argument that was not an object literal, so the most direct form of the bug went unreported.
cases.code:
import { MongoClient } from 'mongodb';
async function f(db, req) { return db.collection('u').find(req.body); }

cases.title: The same lookup with the value pinned to a string
cases.rationale: Coercing to a primitive removes the operator surface entirely. The fix, and it must stay quiet.
cases.code:
import { MongoClient } from 'mongodb';
async function f(db, req) { return db.collection('u').find({ name: String(req.body.name) }); }

cases.title: A module-scope constant reported as user input
cases.rationale: An object built from a `const` string in the same file. Nothing here is caller-controlled. Reported until 2026-08-30 with the message `User input "NAME" is used directly`, because any bare identifier in a filter counted as user input. That one heuristic produced this false positive and the miss in ILB-0121 together.

cases.title: A vendor secret key committed as a literal
cases.rationale: `sk_live_` is Stripe's published prefix for a live secret key. The name of the binding is irrelevant — the FORMAT is somebody else's contract, so the finding does not depend on what a project calls its variables.
cases.code: const anything = 'sk_live_FAKE_LIVE_KEY_FOR_TESTING_PURPOSES_ONLY_123456';

cases.title: The same key read from the environment
cases.rationale: The literal is gone; the name is unchanged. A rule keying on the NAME still reports this, which is the false positive the format check exists to avoid.
cases.code: const apiKey = process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY;

cases.title: A publishable key, which is meant to be in the bundle
cases.rationale: `pk_live_` is the half Stripe documents as safe to ship to a browser. Reporting it teaches consumers to disable the rule.
cases.code: const publishable = 'pk_live_FAKE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY_FOR_TESTING_ONLY_123456';

cases.title: Nested quantifier over an overlapping character class
cases.rationale: `(a+)+$` is the textbook catastrophic backtrack: the inner and outer quantifiers can partition the same input exponentially many ways, so a non-matching string of length n costs 2^n steps.
cases.code: const re = /^(a+)+$/;

cases.title: The same intent written without nesting
cases.rationale: One quantifier over one class matches the same language in linear time.
cases.code: const re = /^a+$/;

cases.title: Nested quantifiers over DISJOINT classes
cases.rationale: `(a+b+)+` nests, but the classes cannot overlap, so there is only one way to partition any input and no backtracking explosion. A rule matching the SHAPE rather than the ambiguity reports it.
cases.code: const re = /^(a+b+)+$/;

cases.title: A reactive value missing from the dependency array
cases.rationale: The effect closes over `userId` and declares no dependency on it, so it keeps the value from the render in which it first ran. React's own docs call this the stale-closure bug; the symptom is a screen that silently shows another user's data after navigation.
cases.code:
import { useEffect } from 'react';
export function C({ userId }) { useEffect(() => { load(userId); }, []); return null; }

cases.title: The same effect with the value declared
cases.rationale: Adding the dependency is the whole fix, and it must stay quiet.
cases.code:
import { useEffect } from 'react';
export function C({ userId }) { useEffect(() => { load(userId); }, [userId]); return null; }

cases.title: A ref read inside an effect that declares nothing
cases.rationale: `useRef` returns a stable object, so React explicitly tells you NOT to list it. A rule treating every closed-over binding as reactive reports this, and reporting it teaches consumers to add a dependency React documents as wrong.
cases.code:
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
export function C() { const r = useRef(null); useEffect(() => { look(r.current); }, []); return null; }

cases.title: Model output written straight into the DOM
cases.rationale: A model's text is attacker-influenced whenever any part of the prompt is. Writing it to `innerHTML` makes prompt injection into stored XSS — OWASP's LLM02 in its shortest form.
cases.code:
import { generateText } from 'ai';
async function f(el, prompt) { const { text } = await generateText({ model: m, prompt }); el.innerHTML = text; }

cases.title: The same output assigned as text
cases.rationale: `textContent` cannot introduce markup. The fix, and it must stay quiet.
cases.code:
import { generateText } from 'ai';
async function f(el, prompt) { const { text } = await generateText({ model: m, prompt }); el.textContent = text; }

cases.title: A local string written to innerHTML in a file that also calls a model
cases.rationale: The sink is real but the value never touched the model. A rule keying on 'this file imports the AI SDK and something reaches innerHTML' reports it.
cases.code:
import { generateText } from 'ai';
async function f(el) { const label = 'Loading…'; el.innerHTML = label; }

cases.title: Two modules importing each other
cases.rationale: `a` imports `b`, `b` imports `a`. At runtime one of them observes the other half-initialised, so a `const` is `undefined` at module-evaluation time and the failure appears far from its cause. Needs real files: a cycle is a property of the module GRAPH, so a single source string cannot express one — the fixture pair under benchmarks/cases/fixtures/cycle exists for that reason.
cases.code:
import { b } from './b';
export const a = b;

cases.title: The same import, to a module that imports nothing back
cases.rationale: Structurally identical at the import site — same syntax, same directory, same resolver work. Only the far end differs, which is what makes it the decoy: a rule that reports on 'this file imports a sibling' rather than on the graph reports this too.
cases.code:
import { leaf } from './leaf';
export const a = leaf;

cases.title: Allocation sized by a request, on a handler whose parameter is not spelled req
cases.rationale: `Buffer.allocUnsafe(capacity)` where `capacity` comes from `req.query.capacity`. The rule recognised the request by the root identifier's SPELLING, against REQUEST_ROOTS = ['req','request','ctx','event'], so the identical handler written `(inbound, outbound)` — or TypeScript's own `(request: Request, response: Response)` renamed on the way in — allocated from a peer-chosen size and reported nothing. The rename probe found 18 true positives that went silent this way, with `.query.capacity` still in plain sight one link up. Fixed 2026-08-30 by asking readsRequestShape before walking to the root.

cases.title: A log line named message reported as bytes off the wire
cases.rationale: WIRE_NAMES hardcoded ['chunk','chunks','buffer','buf','payload','frame','packet','raw','message','msg'] with no way for a consumer to disagree. A project whose `message` is a log line, or whose `raw` is a template string, was reported on the word alone and could do nothing about it — an additive option can grow the list but never remove the word we guessed wrong about. Fixed 2026-08-30 by making wireNames, requestRootNames and countNames REPLACE their defaults; `wireNames: []` turns the name arm off entirely.
cases.code: function f(message) { return Buffer.alloc(message.length); }

cases.title: An error code containing an abbreviation reported as a credential
cases.rationale: auth0/express-openid-connect lib/errors.js:25 declares MTLS_INCOMPATIBLE_CLIENT_AUTH: 'mtls_incompatible_client_auth'. isNaturalWordString requires every 3+ character token to carry a vowel, and 'mtls' does not — nor do jwt, xhr, sql, ssh. One abbreviation among four dictionary words made the whole identifier read as opaque, and an error code was reported at CWE-798 CVSS 9.8 CRITICAL tagged SOC2 PCI-DSS HIPAA GDPR, inside an authentication library. Found 2026-09-01, the first hour the corpus scan could see again after #811.
cases.code: const codes = Object.freeze({ MTLS_INCOMPATIBLE_CLIENT_AUTH: 'mtls_incompatible_client_auth' });

cases.title: A build-tool path template reported as a credential
cases.rationale: okta/okta-auth-js jest.cjs.js:15 declares const OktaAuth = '<rootDir>/build/cjs/exports/default.js'. isUrlOrPath accepts a scheme or a leading slash; Jest writes <rootDir>/ and webpack writes [name]/, and the templated root is not a segment it can parse — so the value never reached the path guard and a module map entry was reported at CWE-798 CVSS 9.8 CRITICAL. Only the ROOT token is stripped and the remainder must still pass the segment test, so an opaque segment after a template root is still a credential.
cases.code: const OktaAuth = '<rootDir>/build/cjs/exports/default.js';

cases.title: Diffie-Hellman key agreement on the 768-bit MODP group
cases.rationale: A named MODP group is a fixed prime, and the expensive step of breaking Diffie-Hellman depends on the prime rather than the session. One precomputation therefore reads every session that used the group, which is the Logjam result: `modp1` is 768-bit and fell to an academic budget. The plugin declared crypto as its surface and named no Diffie-Hellman API at all until this rule.

cases.title: createDiffieHellman given a prime chosen elsewhere states no strength
cases.rationale: The string/Buffer overload of `createDiffieHellman` supplies a prime that was decided somewhere else. Nothing at the call site says how large it is, so a structural rule that reported here would be guessing, and the author would have no edit that satisfies it. Recorded as a case so the silence is measured rather than assumed.

cases.title: Supabase service_role key inlined into the browser bundle
cases.rationale: `service_role` bypasses Row Level Security entirely — it is a database superuser in a string. A `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix exists to inline a value into the client bundle at build time, so the two together publish unrestricted read and write on every table. The line is indistinguishable from any other `createClient` call, which is why review does not catch it.
cases.code:
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js';
export const db = createClient(url, process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY);

cases.title: Supabase RPC executed under a caller-supplied function name
cases.rationale: `.rpc(name)` runs a Postgres function by name over PostgREST. When the name is computed the caller chooses which function executes, and an exposed schema routinely holds privileged helpers beside the intended one. Same shape as a dynamic `require()`: the danger is that the callee is data.
cases.code:
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js';
export const run = (db, req) => db.rpc(req.query.fn, req.body);

cases.retired: 2026-10-12 FP/FN audit: the case's code is fail-closed. On failure getUser() resolves { data: { user: null } }, so `if (!data.user) throw` takes the deny branch — the documented Supabase pattern, not an authentication bypass. The rule no longer reports a guarded identity; the unsafe shape (testing the always-truthy `data` container) is ILB-0165, and this shape is pinned silent as ILB-0166.
cases.title: Supabase auth failure read as an anonymous request
cases.rationale: `getUser()` reports a missing, expired or forged token by RETURNING `error`, not by throwing. Destructuring only `data` makes an authentication failure and an anonymous request indistinguishable, because `user` is null on both paths — so a downstream `if (!user)` guard cannot tell them apart.

cases.title: Supabase storage bucket created public
cases.rationale: A public bucket serves every object in it to anyone holding the URL: no session, no RLS check, no expiry. It is a decision about the bucket's whole future contents, taken once at creation, long before the file that should not have been public is uploaded. Object names are guessable more often than teams expect.
cases.code:
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js';
await db.storage.createBucket('user-documents', { public: true });

cases.title: CLI command registered with no description
cases.rationale: burgee F3. A command with no description is a bare word in --help, --schema and an MCP tool list; an agent has to run it to learn what it does (yargs #877, #1047).

cases.title: Runnable CLI command with no example
cases.rationale: burgee F3 and H2. The example is the one part of help an agent can act on without reading prose. A runnable yargs command whose builder declares no .example() shows none in `serve --help` (yargs #877, #1640).
cases.code:
import yargs from 'yargs';
yargs(process.argv.slice(2)).command('serve', 'Start the server', (y) => y.option('port', {}), serve);

cases.title: console.log inside a CLI command handler
cases.rationale: burgee O3. --json (O1) and quiet non-TTY output (O2) only hold if every byte goes through one output layer; a console.log in a handler is prose inside a JSON document (oclif/core #1644).

cases.title: Prompt in a CLI command with no flag behind it
cases.rationale: burgee P1. A prompt that no flag can answer hangs or fails every non-interactive caller — an agent, CI, a pipe (clack #167, oclif/oclif #1492).

cases.title: A job queue that owns .command() and .action()
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. `.command()`, `.action()` and `console.log` are ordinary names; with commander imported in the same file, the receiver here is still not commander's. Only binding resolution keeps the CLI-floor rules quiet on it.
cases.code:
import 'commander';
queue.command('email').action((job) => { console.log(job); });

cases.title: A prompt whose value a flag supplies first
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. The prompt is the right operand of `??` on the handler's own options parameter, so a caller who passes --name never sees it.

cases.title: A tool argument joined onto a root and read from disk
cases.rationale: path.join(ROOT, p) still resolves `../../.ssh/id_rsa` outside ROOT; nothing confines the joined path before fs reads it — the EscapeRoute class (CVE-2025-53109 / CVE-2025-53110).

cases.title: A tool fetches the URL the model chose
cases.rationale: The URL is a tool argument, so a steered model can make the server request the cloud metadata endpoint or an internal admin port and read the answer back.

cases.title: An SDK v1 Streamable HTTP transport on a raw express app, with no DNS-rebinding protection
cases.rationale: The v1 transport leaves enableDnsRebindingProtection off by default, the app is a raw express() with no Host validation, and it listens on every interface: any web page the user opens can rebind its hostname to the server and call its tools.

cases.title: A tool argument interpolated into pg query text
cases.rationale: The SQL text carries the argument, so `x' OR '1'='1` reads every row; parameterisation would keep it in the values array.

cases.title: One stateless transport and server shared by every request
cases.rationale: In stateless mode (sessionIdGenerator: undefined) a module-level transport serves every client, so one client's response can be delivered to another (CVE-2026-25536).

cases.title: A counter as the MCP session id
cases.rationale: Session ids are sequential, so any client can guess another's id and attach to its session.

cases.title: A calculator tool that evals the expression
cases.rationale: The expression is a tool argument and eval runs it with the server's privileges: require('child_process').execSync('id') is a valid expression.

cases.title: A tool returns the whole process environment to the model
cases.rationale: JSON.stringify(process.env) hands every credential the server was started with to the model, its host log, and anything that can steer it.

cases.title: An MCP client joins listTools() descriptions into the system prompt
cases.rationale: Tool descriptions are written by whoever runs the MCP server; spliced into `system` a poisoned description carries the host's own authority (tool poisoning).

cases.title: A project-local .mcp.json chooses the command a stdio client spawns
cases.rationale: The config is read from the repository the user opened, so the repository author chooses the process the MCP client spawns (the MCPoison / CVE-2025-6514 class).

cases.title: Two registrations give one server the same tool name
cases.rationale: McpServer throws on the second registration, so the server crashes at startup, or behind a try/catch silently keeps the first handler.

cases.title: Supabase auth result trusted through its always-truthy container
cases.rationale: `getUser()` resolves `{ data: { user: null }, error }` on a missing, expired or forged token. `data` is an object on both paths, so a branch on `data` instead of `data.user` (or `error`) grants the authenticated path to a failed authentication.

cases.title: Supabase auth identity guarded fail-closed without reading error
cases.rationale: On failure the identity is null, so `if (!user)` denies: the documented Supabase pattern is fail-closed, and reporting it as CWE-287 is a false positive (found in supabase/supabase examples and vercel/nextjs-subscription-payments).

cases.title: A hidden array element behind an invisible Hangul filler
cases.rationale: U+3164 HANGUL FILLER is a letter, so JavaScript accepts it as a whole identifier, but every editor draws it as nothing. Placed after the comma it is a third array element that a reviewer cannot see, and in the middle of a name (`adm<U+3164>in`) it mints a second binding that renders as the first. The parser reads it correctly; the weakness is entirely in what the human can see (the published 'invisible backdoor' technique).

cases.title: Template auto-escaping switched off for the whole engine
cases.rationale: `escapeMarkup = false` makes the template engine interpolate every value as raw HTML. The decision is taken once, on one line, far from every template it affects, so no review of an individual template sees it; after it, any user-controlled value rendered through the engine is a stored or reflected XSS sink.

cases.title: Upload interceptor with no file size limit
cases.rationale: multer enforces only the limits it is given and `fileSize` defaults to Infinity; NestJS adds defaults for field-name limits and none for size. A route behind a bare `FileInterceptor('file')` stores however many bytes the client sends, in memory with the default storage. Seen in 11 of 79 NestJS repositories measured.

cases.title: Upload interceptor that bounds the file size
cases.rationale: The same route with `limits.fileSize` set on the interceptor: multer aborts the upload at the limit, so the allocation is bounded. Reporting it would be asking for a limit that is already there.

cases.title: a Node.js builtin loaded without the node: scheme where the codebase requires it
cases.rationale: Under `enforce-node-protocol-usage: ['always']` every builtin is spelled `node:x`, so no same-named package in node_modules can shadow it. A bare `fs` breaks the convention the option states.
cases.code: import fs from 'fs';

cases.title: webpack loaders configured inside an import specifier
cases.rationale: `style!css!./a.css` ties the module to webpack and hides its loader chain from the webpack config, where every other loader is declared.
cases.code: import css from 'style!css!./app.css';

cases.title: A comment written between JSX tags
cases.rationale:
`
// TODO
` has no comment in it: JSX has no comment syntax between tags, so the characters render on the page. The comment belongs in braces.
cases.code:
export const a =
// TODO: remove
;

cases.title: A JSX tag that names no binding
cases.rationale: `<Foo />` compiles to a reference to `Foo`. With no import or declaration providing it, the page throws a ReferenceError when it renders.
cases.code: export const a = <Foo />;

cases.title: React imported only for classic-runtime JSX
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. `import React from 'react'` looks unused because no identifier names it, but classic-runtime JSX compiles to `React.createElement`. `jsx-uses-react` marks it used for `no-unused-vars`, so the rule itself never reports.
cases.code:
import React from 'react';
export const a = <div />;

cases.title: A component used only as a JSX tag
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. `import App from './App'` looks unused because no expression names it, but `<App />` is a use. `jsx-uses-vars` marks it used for `no-unused-vars`, so the rule itself never reports.
cases.code:
import App from './App';
export const a = <App />;

cases.title: A rule a tool can enforce, written as prose in a skill
cases.rationale: "do not rebase" is a rule a hook or lint check can hold. Written as a sentence it is a suggestion the model may skip, and it costs context in every session that loads the skill.
cases.code: Merge with `git merge origin/main`; do not rebase.

cases.title: A seven-step procedure in always-loaded memory
cases.rationale: A numbered procedure is loaded into every session but used in one kind of task. It belongs in a skill, which loads only when its trigger matches.
cases.code:
Release:

1. Step 1
2. Step 2
3. Step 3
4. Step 4
5. Step 5
6. Step 6
7. Step 7

cases.title: The same guidance line in AGENTS.md and GEMINI.md
cases.rationale: Files in one directory chain load together, so a line in two of them is paid for twice, and the copies drift when one is edited. The case is a GEMINI.md beside the fixture AGENTS.md under benchmarks/cases/fixtures/guidance, copying its one rule line.
cases.code: - **Run the full test suite** before you ask anyone to review the branch.

cases.title: A subagent with no model declared
cases.rationale: A subagent with no `model` inherits the caller's, so a review or search agent silently runs on the most expensive model. The declaration is the cost decision.
cases.code: Review the diff.

cases.title: A style prop written as a CSS string
cases.rationale: `style="color: red"` is HTML. React throws at render time, because its `style` prop takes an object of CSS properties. The mistake is common when markup is pasted into JSX.
cases.code: <div style="color: red" />

cases.title: A component named with an underscore
cases.rationale: `<My_component />` is a component reference that is not PascalCase. The naming convention is what tells readers, and tools, a tag is a component, and it is what `eslint-config-react-app` enforces.
cases.code: <My_component />

cases.title: Reading another component's propTypes
cases.rationale: Production builds strip `propTypes`, so `Foo.propTypes` is `undefined` there and anything built from it breaks only in production.
cases.code: const shape = Foo.propTypes;

cases.title: A proxied upload request with no error listener
cases.rationale: `http.request` returns a ClientRequest. A refused connection emits 'error'; with no listener Node throws it from the event loop, so the try/catch around the await never sees it and the process exits. Found in parse-server's GraphQL createFile, 2026-11-24.

cases.title: A spawned process with no error listener
cases.rationale: `spawn` emits 'error' when the binary is missing or the cwd is bad. A close listener does not handle it, and a surrounding try/catch cannot catch an event. Found in Eleventy's spawnAsync, 2026-11-24: a machine without git kills the build.

cases.title: exec with no error listener
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. Node attaches its own 'error' listener inside exec and execFile, with or without a callback, so a missing binary or bad cwd cannot crash the process. Checked on Node 24. A rule that reported it would claim a crash that cannot happen.
cases.code:
import { exec } from 'node:child_process';
exec('git log');

cases.title: An emoji in a span with no label
cases.rationale: NOT a defect: a deprecated no-op stub kept so jsx-a11y configs naming it load. Upstream's `accessible-emoji` asked for `role="img"` and an `aria-label`, and is deprecated there; this rule never reports.
cases.code: export const a = 🐼;

cases.title: A label with no id or nesting
cases.rationale: NOT a defect: a deprecated no-op stub kept so jsx-a11y configs naming it load. Upstream's `label-has-for` is replaced by `label-has-associated-control`, which does the checking; this rule never reports.
cases.code: export const a = <label>Name</label>;

cases.title: A select with an onChange handler
cases.rationale: NOT a defect: a deprecated no-op stub kept so jsx-a11y configs naming it load. Upstream's `no-onchange` asked for `onBlur`, and is deprecated there; this rule never reports.
cases.code: export const a = <select onChange={go}><option /></select>;

cases.title: An import after a statement, written under the deprecated name
cases.rationale: eslint-plugin-import 2.32.0's deprecated `imports-first` is `first` under another name. A config naming it must load and report what `first` reports: an import that follows a non-import statement, since imports are hoisted and the file should say so.
cases.code: import foo from 'foo'; const a = 1; import bar from 'bar';

cases.title: A generated secret picked with a random byte reduced by a divisor that does not divide 256
cases.rationale: crypto.randomBytes yields bytes uniform over 0..255. `b % allChars.length` with a 70-character alphabet maps 256 values onto 70 slots, so the first 46 characters come up 4 times in 256 and the other 24 only 3 times: part of the generated password is a third more likely than the rest. ToolJet's generateTJDBPasswordForRole built the body of a database password this way before ToolJet/ToolJet#19245 replaced it with crypto.randomInt.
cases.code: import crypto from 'node:crypto'; const allChars = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789!@#$%^&*'; const remaining = Array.from(crypto.randomBytes(26)).map((b) => allChars[b % allChars.length]);

cases.title: A function that recurses down error.cause with no visited set or depth bound
cases.rationale: `cause` is an ordinary property, so a cycle (`e.cause = e`, or two errors citing each other) is one assignment away, and the walk then throws RangeError from inside the code that was handling the first error. Node.js lib/internal/assert/assertion_error.js copyError recursed on source.cause with no memo (nodejs/node#67572, fixed upstream with a map of copies).
cases.code: function copyError(source) { const target = Object.assign({}, source); let { cause } = source; if (isError(cause)) cause = copyError(cause); target.cause = cause; return target; }

cases.title: decodeURIComponent on a request parameter outside a try that catches
cases.rationale: decodeURIComponent and decodeURI throw URIError on a `%` that does not start a valid escape (`p%ss`, `%E0%A4%A`, a bare `%`). On a route parameter a client chooses, that is a 500 on demand, or a dead process outside a framework error boundary. Constructed from the rule's intent (docs/intents/a-uri-decode-on-request-input-is-a-crash); not observed in a third-party repository.
cases.code: app.get('/f/:name', (req, res) => res.send(decodeURIComponent(req.params.name)));

cases.title: gRPC server reflection registered on the public server with no guard
cases.rationale: Reflection answers 'which services does this listener serve?' to any client, unauthenticated. Registered unconditionally it ships to production, and `grpcurl list` names every service on the server, the internal ones a team assumed nobody knew about included. Observed in the security-research grpc-2 lab.

cases.title: gRPC server reflection registered only in development
cases.rationale: The reference fix for the grpc-2 lab: reflection is registered inside a branch on the environment, so production never serves it. A rule that reported this would be asking for something the code already did.
cases.code:
import { ReflectionService } from '@grpc/reflection';
if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development') new ReflectionService(def).addToServer(server);

cases.title: gRPC caller identity taken from a forwarded metadata header
cases.rationale: A backend behind a gateway trusts an identity header the gateway is supposed to set. Metadata is HTTP/2 headers and the client sets all of them, so once the backend is reachable another way anyone can claim to be anyone. Observed in the security-research grpc-1 lab.

cases.title: gRPC caller resolved from a server-side token table
cases.rationale: The reference fix for the grpc-1 lab: the presented token is a key into a table the server owns, so the caller is whatever the server says the token belongs to. A rule that reported this would be asking for something the code already did.

cases.title: gRPC receive cap removed with -1
cases.rationale: gRPC defaults the receive cap to 4 MiB. Setting grpc.max_receive_message_length to -1 removes it, so one request can make the server buffer any size before a handler runs.
cases.code: const server = new grpc.Server({ 'grpc.max_receive_message_length': -1 });

cases.title: gRPC receive cap raised but bounded
cases.rationale: A 16 MiB cap is a deliberate, bounded raise. A rule that reported every non-default cap would be reporting configuration, not a defect.
cases.code: const server = new grpc.Server({ 'grpc.max_receive_message_length': 16 * 1024 * 1024 });

cases.title: Caught error stack sent as gRPC status details
cases.rationale: Status details travel to the client. Built from a caught error's stack they disclose file paths, dependency versions and whatever the error quoted.

cases.title: Generic gRPC status details, real error logged
cases.rationale: The remedy: the caught error is logged server-side and the client gets a fixed message.

cases.title: Recursive merge guarded by a Set#has denylist of the three prototype keys
cases.rationale: `if (FORBIDDEN.has(key)) continue;` against a module `const` Set holding __proto__, constructor and prototype rejects every key that reaches Object.prototype, exactly as the `key === '__proto__' || …` spelling does. Found dogfooding the protocol-ctf ws-3 fixed server (ofri-peretz/security-research, protocol-ctf/docs/SCANNER-RESULTS.md run 2), reported as massAssignment.

cases.title: A placeholder literal serialised by JSON.stringify and sent over a WebSocket
cases.rationale: `'<redacted>'` reaches `ws.send` only as a value JSON.stringify quotes; it is author-written JSON data, not markup being composed, and the code has no sanitization step to be improper. Found dogfooding the protocol-ctf ws-2 server (ofri-peretz/security-research, protocol-ctf/docs/SCANNER-RESULTS.md run 2).
